Photograph: Kevin Fujii/AP Weather tracker Hurricanes Analysis Weather tracker: Hurricane Lowell pounds Hawaii’s western islands Megan Davies for MetDesk Widespread damage across Ni‘ihau, Kauaʻi and O‘ahu, while in Japan further heavy rainfall causes widespread flooding Fri 11 Sep 2026 04.05 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 06.17 EDT Share Hurricane Lowell caused significant damage to Hawaii’s western islands this week. On Tuesday night the centre of Lowell tracked 50 miles (80km) from the island of Ni‘ihau in Kauai county as a category 2 storm with winds of up to 110mph. The strong winds resulted in widespread power outages across Ni’ihau, and the islands of Kauaʻi and O‘ahu. The event was particularly notable because a tornado watch had been issued for Kauaʻi on Monday night and into Tuesday morning. According to research maps from Iowa State University, it was likely to be the first tornado watch in Hawaii’s history. In the event, a tornado was not documented, however hurricanes can produce tornadoes and most often occur in thunderstorms within rain bands away from the centre of the hurricane. Currently, five named stormed have occurred in the central Pacific with the strong El Niño this year being a key driver in the above normal hurricane season, as noted by the National Weather Service. View image in fullscreen A large wave crashes on the shore caused by Hurricane Lowell on the westside of Hawaii’s Oʻahu island. Photograph: Craig Fujii/AP In Asia, further heavy rainfall in Japan has caused flooding of roads and subway stations, disrupting services including the main bullet train Tokaido Shinkansen. A record-breaking 104.5mm of rain fell within an hour through Tuesday afternoon in Nagoya. The heavy downfall occurred because of a stationary front and moist air mass associated with tropical depression Krovanh, resulting in extremely unstable conditions. A level-two advisory remained in place for landslides on Friday across the country. Some landslides have already occurred, including one of the main starting points for Mount Fuji on Wednesday, covering three vehicles in debris. No injuries or fatalities were reported. Heavy rainfall also hit large parts central-southern Europe in recent days. Earlier this week, cooler air pushed south-east across much of the continent, displacing the warm air mass behind southern Europe’s late season heatwave. The boundary between the two air masses, a cold front, reached the Mediterranean by Wednesday. There, the front helped create ideal conditions for violent thunderstorms: cool air moving over the Mediterranean’s unusually warm waters created an unstable atmosphere, while the sea supplied plenty of moisture. As a result, large thunderstorms formed over the waters around Corsica, Sardinia and northern Italy on Wednesday and Thursday, producing torrential rainfall and flash flooding, strong winds, as well as a few tornados. At a weather station in Veneto, 154.2mm of rain was recorded in just 3.5 hours. The storms pushed north-east into Austria and the Balkans late on Thursday with a few forecast to continue into Friday. However, this wet weather is not expected to persist in the region over the weekend and into the start of next week, with drier and sunnier weather likely to develop. https://www.dw.com/en/torrential-rain-an.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NjCg People watch the swollen Besos River after it exceeded its danger level following torrential rain near Barcelona Image: Kike Rincón/Europa Press/abaca/picture alliance Advertisement Two people were reported dead on Sunday, with at least one person missing, after torrential rain triggered flooding in Spain's northeastern Catalonia region . Authorities have warned of an "extreme danger" in parts of Barcelona and Girona, with rivers at risk of overflowing and residents in some areas urged to stay indoors. What do we know about the victims? One person died when a wall collapsed at a campsite in Tordera, north of Barcelona, while another drowned in a flooded garage in Montornes del Valles, Catalan firefighters said. Emergency services were also searching for a missing person in Pineda de Mar, about 52 kilometers (32 miles) north of Barcelona. Catalan regional leader Salvador Illa urged residents to exercise "the greatest caution" and follow instructions from emergency services. How badly has Catalonia been hit? More than 100 millimeters (3.9 inches) of rain fell overnight in numerous locations, according to Spain's AEMET weather agency. Civil protection authorities sent alerts to people living near the Besos River warning of a risk of it bursting its banks. Residents were told to move to upper floors if flooding occurred. Homes were flooded and vehicles submerged in towns near Barcelona, while local rail services were disrupted. Emergency crews rescued people trapped in vehicles on flooded streets in Granollers and other communities. Heavy storms in eastern Spain cause major floods To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Flights at Barcelona airport were also canceled or delayed, while shops closed early and sporting and cultural events were called off. What is causing the extreme weather? The storms are linked to a weather phenomenon known in Spain as a DANA, traditionally called a "gota fria," or "cold drop." It occurs when cold air high in the atmosphere meets warm, moisture-laden air rising from the Mediterranean, producing intense thunderstorms. Spain 's geography can amplify the effect, as moist air from the Mediterranean is forced upwards by mountain ranges separating the coast from the country's elevated interior. The latest flooding comes almost two years after catastrophic floods linked to a DANA killed 238 people in eastern Spain, mostly in Valencia , in October 2024. A study published in 2026 found that human-caused climate change intensified the rainfall during that disaster. The findings apply only to the 2024 Valencia floods , and a separate analysis would be needed to determine the influence of climate change on the latest flooding in Catalonia. https://www.baltictimes.com/lithuanian_c.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Lithuanian Catholic Church to investigate crimes against minors, vulnerable adults 2026-09-28 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Lithuania's Bishops' Conference has decided to launch an investigation into crimes committed against minors and vulnerable adults within the Catholic Church since 1990. According to the organisation, consultations will be held with the Holy See and Lithuanian law enforcement authorities regarding the nature of the inquiry. The bishops said the probe aims to support victims, strengthen prevention of such crimes and create a safer environment within the Church. They emphasised that the priority is the victim, rather than the institution's reputation. In September, courts opened criminal cases against two priests involving crimes related to children. Priest Tadas Svedavicius is accused of sexual offences against 11 minors. Law enforcement data indicates 34 criminal episodes, with the suspected crimes allegedly committed between 2002 and 2025. The case has been referred to the Vilnius Regional Court. In a separate case, priest Rysardas Peciunas is charged with possession of child pornography. There are no victims in this specific case. Following the charges against Svedavicius and Peciunas, discussions have intensified in Lithuania regarding the establishment of a public sex offender registry.
